The ferry terminal at North Point closed shortly after six on Tuesday morning, when the harbourmaster reported that the swell had pushed past the outer breakwater. Crews spent the next several hours securing the ramps and moving the ticket machines to higher ground. By midday the water had reached the loading lane, and the pumps could no longer keep pace with it.

Passengers who had booked the morning crossing were redirected to the inland bus service, which added four extra departures from the depot on Mill Street. Several families waited in the rain under the awning while staff handed out blankets from a storage locker behind the office. A spokesperson for the operator said the decision had been taken before dawn, after a forecast warned of gusts above fifty knots.

The storm also brought down two power lines along the coastal road, leaving about eleven hundred homes without electricity. Line crews from the regional utility worked through the afternoon, and most customers were reconnected before nightfall. One crew chief described the damage as the worst he had seen in a decade, with several poles leaning at angles that made the wires unsafe to re-energize.

At the processing plant on the eastern side of the bay, managers had been watching the same forecast since Monday evening. The plant handles a large share of the region's farm output, and its cooling systems draw water from the harbour through a channel that sits barely above the normal tide line. During the previous storm, in March, seawater had entered that channel and forced a partial shutdown that took nearly a week to reverse.

This time the managers moved the intake earlier, tested the backup generators, and sent non-essential staff home on Monday afternoon. By Tuesday morning the channel was carrying a mix of seawater and debris, and the filters had begun to clog faster than the maintenance team could clear them. As a result, the plant suspended operations at ten past eight, and hundreds of workers were sent home with instructions to check the staff line for updates.

The port authority has said it will reopen the terminal when the swell drops below two metres and the coastal road is cleared. Forecasters expect the system to move north overnight, although a second front could arrive before the weekend. For the families who spent the morning under the awning, and for the workers waiting at the processing plant, the question now is whether the damage can be repaired before the next tide.
